o: We need students whose `department_id` does not appear in the `Departments` table. In Example 1, departments 14, 33, 74, and 77 are missing, so John, Daiana, Steve, and Jasmine are returned while everyone else is filtered out. This is a classic anti-join problem: keep rows from `Students` that fail to match any row in `Departments`. Constraints are tiny (typical LeetCode DB sizes), so any correct set-based approach works; the real question is which SQL idiom to use.
k: An anti-join keeps left-table rows with no match in the right table — detectable via LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL, NOT IN, or NOT EXISTS.
NOT IN is dangerous if the subquery can return NULLs; here department ids in Departments are non-null primary keys, so it is safe.
NOT EXISTS is generally the most robust and optimizer-friendly idiom for anti-joins.

a.i: Left-join every student onto the Departments table on matching ids. Students whose department exists produce a matched row; students whose department was deleted produce NULL in every Departments column, so filtering on `d.id IS NULL` selects exactly them.
s: LEFT JOIN Departments d ON s.department_id = d.id
Filter rows where d.id IS NULL

c.python:
# LeetCode SQL problem — submit as a MySQL query:
SELECT s.id, s.name
FROM Students s
LEFT JOIN Departments d ON s.department_id = d.id
WHERE d.id IS NULL;

a.t: O(n + m) expected with hash join (or O(n log n + m log m) with sort-merge) where n and m are the sizes of Students and Departments.

a.i: Collect all existing department ids into a subquery and keep only students whose department_id is not in that set. Since `Departments.id` is a primary key it can never be NULL, so the classic NOT IN + NULL pitfall does not apply here.
s: Outer query filters WHERE department_id NOT IN (subquery)
Select id and name from Students
a.t: O(n * m) worst case if the optimizer materializes/linear-scans the list per row; typically O(n + m) with proper optimization.
a.sp: O(m) to hold the materialized id list.

a.i: For each student, check whether any department with that id exists. NOT EXISTS short-circuits on the first match and handles NULL semantics correctly by design, making it the safest and usually fastest portable idiom for anti-joins.
s: Correlated subquery checks existence of a department with id equal to the student's department_id
Keep students where NOT EXISTS returns true
a.t: O(n + m) with an index/hash lookup on Departments.id (primary key), O(n * m) without one.

w: In an interview, lead with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL since it is the most visual explanation of an anti-join, then mention NOT EXISTS as the production-grade choice. Pitfalls: using INNER JOIN (drops exactly the rows we want), forgetting that NOT IN breaks silently when the subquery yields NULLs (safe here only because id is a primary key), and selecting columns from Departments in the output (they are all NULL). Edge cases: empty Departments table (all students returned) or empty Students table (empty result). Follow-ups may ask to also report how many students each deleted department had, or to do this with pandas/SQL window functions.
